 Come Nov. 1, expect Georgia Marketplace plans to rise as much as 30% 
 October 20, 2026 2:31 PM 
 By: 
 Sofi Gratas
 Share this page
 Share this page on Twitter 
 Share this page on Facebook 
 Share this page on Email 
 Share this page on Print 
 republish 
 Primary Content
 Caption 
 Those planning to shop for a healthcare plan during open enrollment on the Affordable Care Act's marketplace beginning Nov. 1. will see premium increases, again. 
 Credit: Sofi Gratas/GPB News
 Open enrollment on the Affordable Care Act marketplace begins Nov. 1. Those planning to shop for a plan will see premium increases, again. 
 Georgians will find eight insurance companies offering Marketplace plans during open enrollment on the state-based marketplace, called Georgia Access. That’s after the departure of UnitedHealthcare and Cigna, and the addition of Antidote Health Plan. 
 For renewing plans, monthly premiums across plans are going up between 10% to 30% for 2027. That’s according to rates filed with the state Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner. 
 That looks like an average premium of around $930 a month before any state or federal savings. 
 Rates vary depending on a payer’s age, location and health condition. Ambetter of Peach State’s Bronze plans, which typically feature lower monthly premiums but higher deductibles, range from around $490 a month to just over $730 a month for consumers from 20 to 45 years old. 
 Similarly, Bronze plans under Oscar Health Plan for the same age range are listed from $520 to $780 a month. 
 In the redacted memos they file along with their proposed rate increases, insurers say they’re raising prices due to things like inflation, high prescription drug costs and the expiration of Enhanced Premium Tax Credits last year. 
 In the memo from Ambetter, for example, the insurer assumes that the expiration of subsidies will cause “healthier individuals who tend to be more price sensitive” to leave the market, “worsening” the average health outcomes, and therefore intensifying the healthcare needs, of the remaining covered population. 
 This year, enrollment Marketplace across the U.S. fell for the first time in seven years . Hundreds of thousands of Georgians have dropped their Marketplace plans since January. 
 “They   just chose to terminate their coverage mid-year,” said Deanna Williams, a certified enrollment assister with Georgians for a Healthy Future. 
 As an assister, Williams helps people find a Marketplace plan that works for them. But she says many of her clients this year have been disappointed with the cost of their plans versus services covered. 
 This is the second year that millions of people will not have access to the enhanced subsidies. With monthly costs back up, Williams worries she’ll see even more people dropping their plans and experiencing gaps in care.
 “Getting   those calls when something bad happens, or they get with one of those diagnosis and they don't have insurance …  I'm definitely concerned about how it's going to work out,” Williams said. 
 Georgia Navigator program sees additional year of cuts 
 Under Georgia’s state-based Marketplace, the state gets money every year from the federal government to fund certified health insurance navigators. Those funds are sent to nonprofits and some healthcare systems in the form of a grant which they can then use for training and outreach throughout the enrollment year. 
 These state-funded navigators are meant to provide unbiased and reliable support to populations who need help sorting through Marketplace health insurance, and finding a plan that best works for them. 
 But the federal government cut funding for the navigator program in 2025 by 90%, bringing down the available budget to $10 million. 
 What’s that meant in Georgia is a dramatic decrease in state-funded navigators. During the 2025 enrollment year, which was also the launch of Georgia Access, the public had access to eight community organizations with navigator programs. 
 In 2026, there was only one. This year, the state only funded two . 
 Also, grant amounts meant to serve an entire year of training and outreach are now a fraction of what they once were. According to records from Georgia’s Office of Insurance, grant amounts this year top out at just $5,000 per organization. 
 That’s compared to prior year awards of between around $200,000 to $2 million per organization.  
 Kim Gibson is the executive director of Disability Link, one of the state-funded navigator programs this enrollment year. They were also funded in 2025. 
 "A lot of people don't want to be dependent on other people to input their information, so we were able to spend time with individuals," Gibson said. "Training them how to maintain and apply for themselves."
 Gibson estimates they’ll only be able to reach a fraction of people this year with such reduced funding. 
 Many people with disabilities are eligible for Medicaid. But Gibson worries about those in the coverage gap: those who work, maybe part-time, and thus make too much to qualify for subsidized insurance but too little to afford high Marketplace premiums. 
 "They’re working, their spouse is working, and the employer's not able to afford the health care coverage," Gibson said. "They’re seeking support through the Marketplace for that kind of thing."
 Already, Gibson’s nonprofit has had to make changes to its own employer-sponsored health insurance. In order to manage a nearly 90% increase in cost, but maintain some sort of option for their employees, Gibson said it's adopted a cheaper plan with higher deductibles.

 Rural Health Reporter
 Sofi Gratas covers rural health and health care for GPB. She joined GPB in June 2022 as a Report for America Corps member.  Her focus is on the crisis facing rural communities that consistently rank near the bottom nationwide in health and health care.  Sofi is a 2020 graduate of the University of Georgia's Grady School of Journalism. Prior to joining GPB, she worked at the Red and Black and WUGA.
